reason: The sources provide multiple corroborated claims across independent sites regarding the Moon's origin, synchronous rotation, surface conditions, toxic levitating dust, and water discoveries.
story: Born roughly 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized protoplanet collided with early Earth, the Moon is far stranger than the quiet silver disk in our sky. It is locked in synchronous rotation, matching its 27-day spin to its orbit and showing Earth only one face, though its far side receives just as much sunlight as the near side. While its gravitational pull drives Earth's ocean tides, the Moon is slowly spiraling away by about an inch each year. Down on its surface, where gravity is just one-sixth of Earth's, an abrasive dust layer called regolith coats the ground. Solar radiation charges this razor-sharp dust, causing it to levitate across the landscape. The dust smells like burnt gunpowder and caused allergic reactions in all twelve astronauts who walked on the lunar surface. Yet beneath this harsh vacuum exosphere, permanently shadowed craters harbor ancient water ice.
angle: The Moon's razor-sharp surface dust smells like burnt gunpowder, levitates under solar radiation, and gave every single astronaut who walked on the lunar surface allergic lunar hay fever.

claims.claim: The Moon formed after a Mars-sized body collided with the early Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
The newly formed Moon had a global magma ocean that crystallized to create the lunar crust.
The Moon possesses a solid, iron-rich inner core with a radius of approximately 240 kilometers.
The Moon is tidally locked in synchronous rotation, rotating on its axis in the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
Due to synchronous rotation, the Moon permanently keeps the same hemisphere facing toward Earth.
Calling the Moon's far side the 'dark side' is inaccurate because both sides receive equal sunlight over its orbital cycle.
The Moon completes a full cycle of lunar phases from Earth's moving perspective roughly every 29 to 29.5 days.
Gravitational tidal forces from the Moon are the primary driver of Earth's ocean tides.
The Moon is gradually drifting farther away from Earth at a rate of approximately one to one-and-a-half inches per year.
Surface gravity on the Moon is approximately one-sixth of the gravity on Earth.
The lunar surface is covered in a layer of fine, powdery rubble dust known as regolith, with fractured megaregolith underneath.
The dark lunar features called maria are ancient impact basins flooded with basaltic lava between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.
Lunar dust particles carry a distinctive scent resembling burnt or spent gunpowder.
Solar radiation imparts an electrostatic charge to abrasive lunar dust, causing particles to levitate above the surface.
Exactly twelve humans have walked on the surface of the Moon across six Apollo landing missions.
In 2008, India's Chandrayaan-1 mission detected water and hydroxyl molecules on the Moon's surface, concentrated at polar regions.
In October 2020, NASA's SOFIA airborne observatory detected molecular water on the sunlit surface of the Moon.
Earth's satellite was named simply 'the Moon' because humans were unaware other moons existed until Galileo discovered moons orbiting Jupiter in 1610.
The Moon's atmosphere is an extremely thin, nearly vacuum exosphere that provides virtually no protection from radiation or impacts.
The Moon remains the only celestial body beyond Earth that humans have ever visited.

disputed: Exact age of lunar formation: S1 cites isotopic dating indicating 4.35 billion years ago, whereas S2 states about 4.5 billion years ago; a script should state 'between 4.35 and 4.5 billion years ago'.

Crust thickness values: S1 gives an average crustal thickness of about 50 km, while S2 reports 70 km on the near side and 150 km on the far side; a script should cite crust thickness as variable and model-dependent.

Annual recession rate: S1 measures the retreat as 38 mm (1.5 in) per year from laser ranging, while S2 approximates it as 'about an inch'; a script should phrase it as 'roughly an inch to an inch and a half each year'.
